surfaces.part: overlapping plank band (left, repeated every 6 rows)

answer.evidence: The column scan at x=2 repeats a 6-row cycle: a 1-row light tan band (#d6b073) at rows 0, 6 and 12, then 3 rows of plank face, then a reddish row and a dark shadow row. Each light band is only a 1-row lip or plank end, with no multi-row top plane and no ellipse. The post at x=5 is one flat dark column for rows 0-14 with no cap. The right column (x=7) has only 2 light rows at the top, then a vertical face down to row 14. Everything is a vertical face seen head-on, so the main top surface is 1 row at most, which is a rim only. The object reads as a front elevation, not a 3/4 top-and-front view.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate is a thin tiling fence strip of brown planks with dark seams. Its dark edge pixels are 0% neutral, so the outline is tinted dark brown beside the wood, which is correct material-tone work. It has no flat 5x5 areas (0% near-flat). The shading is shallow, though. The whole piece uses only 7 distinct colours, and the planks show about 4 lightness steps, against 5-6 on Beodeul wood. The simple bench and lamp references still carry 14 colours each, and the hedge carries 11 and 9 visible tones per tile. The candidate's 7 visible tones per tile sit below the hedge and well below the stall (17) and well (20). By eye, the planks and nails read as a little thinner and more uniform than the reference wood, with little per-plank grain or highlight variation. Because the fence is a sparse object, this is only a mild shortfall, but it would look slightly flatter next to the references, and with doubt the verdict is fail.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate is a thin, narrow strip of stacked brown planks. Next to the references the strip looks thinner and more uniform, closer to stacked logs than to weathered scrap planks. The whole thing reads as a flat front elevation of planks. It does not read as an open frame with horizontal beams showing top faces, so the frame kind does not fit well.

But the whole piece uses only 7 distinct colours, which gives about 7 visible tones per tile. That is below the hedge (9) and far below the stall (17) and the well (20). The rusty nails and weathering are at most a dot or two, with no per-plank highlights or grain clusters. When in doubt, fail.

Its 7 visible tones per tile are at the level of the hedge (9) but well below the stall (17) and well (20). There are no flat fills (0% near-flat).
